name: Southern Africa
title: The Rainmaker's Kingdom
pitch: Make a sacred king drought-proof, then move his kingdom onto coal and iron.

core.d: Two dolomite springs here never fail in drought. The land is cool, has frost and no malaria, and coal, iron, tin, salt and soda all lie within ~150 km. The kingdom moves here over ~40 years, starting with royal cattle posts.

img.cap: Apies River near its springs, Groenkloof, Pretoria

start.d: He arrives in 1232 on the Limpopo near the Shashe confluence, below the sacred hill where the king lives apart from his people. The valley is hot, dry and malarial, but it has the gold trade and the kingdom's cattle.

img.cap: Mapungubwe Hill, the royal seat, at sunset

facts: Population (region)
~80,000–150,000 across northern South Africa, eastern Botswana and southwest Zimbabwe (guess)
The kingdom
~9,000 people (often quoted, guess); ~2,000–5,000 at the capital
Climate
Hot savanna in the Limpopo valley; cool grassland plateau (highveld) in the south with frost in winter
Rain
Limpopo valley ~350–450 mm a year and very unreliable; Pretoria ~700 mm; almost all of it falls Oct–Mar in thunderstorms
Growing season
Sorghum and millet Nov–Apr; winters are dry, and on the highveld there is frost May–Aug
Disease
Malaria and tsetse fly (which kills cattle) in the low, hot valleys; none on the frosty highveld
Animals kept
Cattle (the measure of wealth), sheep, goats, dogs, chickens. No horses, donkeys or camels; no wheel or plough
Metals
Iron, copper and gold are smelted locally; a little tin and bronze. No steel, no cast iron
Language
Probably an early Shona-like Bantu language at Mapungubwe (uncertain); Khoe and San click languages to the west and south
Writing
None. Arabic is written only at the coast, ~900 km away

land.d: Hot, dry baobab and mopane country with rich floodplain soil along the rivers. Malaria in wet years, tsetse in thick bush. Where the kingdom is now.

img.c: Photo: JJ van Zyl, CC BY-SA 3.0
img.cap: Limpopo–Shashe confluence: sandy riverbeds and floodplain bush

land.rain: ~700–1,500 mm on the south slopes; dry north side
land.d: A long ridge that catches mist and rain, with perennial streams, forest and salt pans at its western end. The nearest reliable water to Mapungubwe.

img.c: Photo: J.J. van Zyl, CC BY-SA 3.0
img.cap: Hanglip peak above the Soutpansberg's forested south slopes

land.d: Sandstone hills with poor sandy soils but clean streams. Home to San hunters; the Waterberg coalfield lies under the plains just west of it.

img.cap: Sandstone hills and bush of the Waterberg

land.d: Warm thornveld on black clay soils that are fertile but hard to hoe. Some malaria in wet years. The rock below holds the world's biggest chrome and platinum deposits.

img.cap: Thornveld and grass at Nylsvley on the Springbok Flats

land.d: A quartzite ridge west of the core with streams in its gorges, small patches of forest and good building stone. Sites for small dams and water-wheels.

img.cap: Mist over the Magaliesberg ridge near Dewetsnek

land.d: Open, nearly treeless grassland with frost in winter and no malaria or tsetse. Huge herds of game, but in 1235 very few farmers, because it is cold and has little firewood. The coal lies underneath.

img.cap: Open highveld grassland with a stream, northern Free State

land.d: The steep edge where the plateau drops to the lowveld: mist, forests, waterfalls and fast rivers. It blocks the direct road to the sea at Delagoa Bay.

img.c: Photo: Bernard DUPONT from FRANCE, CC BY-SA 2.0
img.cap: The escarpment rising sharply above the lowveld bush

land.d: Hot bush full of elephants (ivory) and game. Bad malaria and tsetse, so cattle do poorly. Phalaborwa's copper and iron are here.

img.c: Photo: Chris Eason from London, CC BY 2.0
img.cap: Dense lowveld bush in Kruger National Park

land.d: The biggest river on the highveld, flowing all year, with coal outcropping along its banks near later Vereeniging. Not navigable: rapids, low water in winter.

img.cap: The Vaal River winding through the Vredefort hills

peoples.popText: ~2,000–5,000 at the hill and the town below (estimates vary)
peoples.culture: Cattle-keeping farmers ruled by a sacred king who lives on the hill and brings rain. Commoners live below. Gold, ivory and copper go to the coast; glass beads and cloth come back. Likely an early Shona-like language (uncertain).
peoples.d: The power he must serve, not rival. The king's standing rides on rain, so water stored in the king's name is the way in.

img.c: Photo: Francesco Bandarin, CC BY-SA 3.0 igo
img.cap: Mapungubwe Hill rising from the dry valley floor

peoples.popText: ~2,000–4,000 in dozens of villages around the capital (guess)
peoples.culture: Commoner homesteads that farm the floodplain and herd cattle, ruled by headmen loyal to the king. Older town K2 (~1,500 people around 1200) emptied when the elite moved to the hill ~1220.
peoples.d: Where he starts as a nobody. The first ORS, wells and cattle-doctoring happen here, among people with little to lose.

peoples.n: Mapela Hill and other hill seats
peoples.culture: Lesser elite seats of the same culture on terraced hills in southwest Zimbabwe and the Tuli area of Botswana (such as Mmamagwa). Chiefs tied to the Mapungubwe king.
peoples.d: Junior chiefs whose loyalty decides whether the kingdom holds together. Wells and iron ploughs for them buy the king's network.

peoples.culture: Leopard's Kopje and related farming peoples, cousins of Mapungubwe's culture, with cattle, gold-washing and granite hill homesteads. Great Zimbabwe is just starting to rise among them.
peoples.d: The biggest pool of people who already share the culture. Historically many of Mapungubwe's people moved north to them; here the flow can go the other way.

peoples.culture: Cattle herders and sorghum farmers on flat-topped hills, with huge cattle kraals. A ranked set of chiefdoms that declines by ~1300, probably from drought and overgrazing.
peoples.d: A cattle people in slow trouble right next door. When they falter, water and grazing can bring them in whole.

peoples.culture: Farming villages in the well-watered valleys of the range, inside Mapungubwe's trade and gift network. Who their later descendants are is uncertain.
peoples.d: The best-watered land near the start, with salt pans. A natural first step out of the dry valley.

peoples.culture: Farmers named by archaeologists for their 'Eiland' pottery (~1000–1300 AD). Small cattle villages, sorghum, iron, and salt boiled at hot springs. No kings that we know of.
peoples.d: The people living closest to the future core. They make salt and know the local iron, and small chiefs join a strong neighbor easily.

peoples.popText: ~2,000–5,000 (guess); 50+ smelting sites known from this millennium
peoples.culture: Mining and smelting villages working copper and iron at Lolwe Hill since ~770 AD. They trade hoes, axes and copper wire to farmers all around.
peoples.d: Skilled miners and smiths already living in the lowveld. Their furnace know-how is the base he builds on; their malarial home is the drawback.

peoples.culture: Farming and fishing villages on the coastal plain, trading at small ports like Chibuene with passing dhows. Their language and ties are poorly known.
peoples.d: They sit on the road to Delagoa Bay, the second sea gate. Friendship here is needed before any port can be built.

peoples.n: San of the Limpopo and Waterberg
peoples.culture: Hunter-gatherers living in bands of 20–50, with click languages, rock art and deep knowledge of game, plants and water. They trade skins and meat with farmers and are sometimes treated as rainmakers.
peoples.d: Trackers, scouts and guides. Later, ideal first horsemen. They need fair dealing, not land-grabs.

img.c: Photo: Francesco Bandarin, CC BY-SA 3.0 igo
img.cap: San rock paintings of animals near Mapungubwe

peoples.culture: Hunting bands following the great game herds across grassland nearly empty of farmers. Rock shelters in the Magaliesberg and along the rivers.
peoples.d: The only people on the plateau where the core will be. Moving cattle posts onto their hunting grounds needs agreement and trade, or it becomes the first war.

peoples.n: Khoe herders of the Vaal and Orange
peoples.culture: Herders of fat-tailed sheep and cattle, speaking Khoe click languages, moving seasonally along the rivers. Clan chiefs, no towns.
peoples.d: Herders who already understand cattle wealth. Trade partners for sheep and hides, and a bridge to the Cape.

peoples.culture: San and Khoe-speaking foragers of the dry Kalahari, some keeping a few animals. They know every waterhole and pan.
peoples.d: Far west and thinly spread. They know the salt pans and the routes, but there is little land there worth taking.

peoples.popText: ~15,000–50,000 (guess); who their descendants are is debated
peoples.culture: Farmers and herders of the green coastal hills, known from 'Blackburn' and 'Moor Park' pottery (~1050–1500 AD). Small chiefdoms, cattle, sorghum, shellfish. Whether they are the ancestors of the Nguni (Zulu, Xhosa, Swazi) is uncertain.
peoples.d: A big, rain-rich population beyond the escarpment. Not neighbors yet, but a later source of joiners and a rival to watch once their chiefdoms grow.

resources.qty: modern: two springs (Upper and Lower Fountain) give ~42–46 million litres a day; they supplied Pretoria for decades
resources.reach: 1230: flowing at the surface, clean and steady through every drought; no digging needed
resources.d: Why the core is here. Enough clean water for a town of ~100,000+ from day one, plus irrigation for winter wheat.

resources.qty: modern: dolomite rock covers thousands of km² around Pretoria and the Cradle of Humankind, hundreds of metres thick
resources.reach: 1230: bare outcrops on hillsides; break with picks and burn in a wood or coal kiln
resources.d: Lime for mortar, plaster, whitewash, sealed granaries, soil and glass. Also holds the underground water that feeds the springs.

resources.qty: modern: a ~1.1 km crater with a salty soda lake; salt and soda ash were mined commercially until the 1950s
resources.reach: 1230: salt and soda crust on the lake edge in the dry season; Iron Age people already boiled the brine in pots
resources.d: The 'place of salt'. Natural soda ash (washing soda) means glass and soap without any chemical works.

resources.qty: modern: one of the world's largest fluorspar deposits (hundreds of millions of t, guess)
resources.reach: 1230: a hill of fluorite rock at the surface; just dig
resources.d: Flux that makes iron and glass melt easier. Later, the start of fluorine chemistry. Nobody here uses it yet.

resources.qty: modern: billions of t; ~190 km × 60 km, five seams, the main No. 2 seam ~6 m thick, all under 300 m deep. It fed most of South Africa's power for a century
resources.reach: 1230: seams at or near the surface along river valleys and the field's northern edge, in places under <10 m of cover; dig with picks and shovels
resources.d: The heart of the plan. Thick, shallow, good coal on a plateau with almost no trees, so coal is needed for lime, bricks, smithing and then coke iron.

resources.qty: modern: a smaller field (hundreds of millions of t, guess), mined from 1878
resources.reach: 1230: seams showing in the banks of the Vaal River
resources.d: A second coal source right on the plateau's one big river.

resources.qty: modern: ~50 billion t, ~40% of South Africa's coal resources; a quarter could be strip-mined
resources.reach: 1230: buried under sand; small outcrops near later Lephalale only. Mostly a later resource
resources.d: A huge reserve for the far future, halfway between Mapungubwe and the core. High ash; less useful early than Witbank.

resources.qty: modern: tens of millions of t of hard hematite at ~60–62% iron (2012 reserve ~9.5 Mt at 60.6%; with nearby Meletse ~81 Mt resource)
resources.reach: 1230: rich red hematite forms the ridge itself; lumps lie on the slopes. No known Iron Age workings here, so it's open
resources.d: The best iron ore within reach: so rich it can almost go straight into a furnace. Pair it with Witbank coke and Pretoria lime.

resources.qty: modern: billions of t of magnetite in thick bands (also the world's largest vanadium source)
resources.reach: 1230: black magnetite bands crop out along ridges; easy to find, but titanium in the ore makes it very hard to smelt in a simple furnace
resources.d: Huge but stubborn ore. Useful later as a vanadium source for tough steel; early on, stick to Thabazimbi.

resources.qty: modern: small, not measured (guess)
resources.reach: 1230: iron-rich rocks in the local hills; the old village at Broederstroom smelted iron here ~500 AD
resources.d: Enough for local smiths in the first years before the Thabazimbi road exists.

resources.qty: modern: mined 1908–1993; pre-colonial miners took ~1,000 to ~20,000 t of tin ore (estimates differ tenfold)
resources.reach: 1230: cassiterite in shallow open cuts; possibly already mined from the 1000s–1200s (dates disputed)
resources.d: The only big tin source in the region: bronze for bearings, bells and gears, and solder and tin plate later.

resources.qty: modern: a giant open-pit mine from 1965, hundreds of millions of t of low-grade copper ore plus magnetite (guess on tonnage)
resources.reach: 1230: worked since ~770 AD; shafts up to 20 m deep, green copper ore and magnetite at the surface of the hill
resources.d: Copper for wire, batteries and brass, with a skilled mining people already there. But it sits in malarial lowveld, far from the core.

resources.qty: modern: one of the world's big phosphate rock deposits, mined since the 1950s
resources.reach: 1230: apatite rock at the surface around the same hill; crush it and treat with acid (later), or use it raw on soil (weak)
resources.d: The fertilizer that makes the poor highveld soils productive once sulfuric acid exists.

resources.qty: modern: mined 1905–1990s, a mid-sized district (guess on tonnage)
resources.reach: 1230: old surface workings already exist; miners use stone hammers and iron wedges, smelters stand on the ridges
resources.d: The copper closest to Mapungubwe (~70 km). First source of copper in the early years.

resources.qty: modern: small hot salty springs (guess on yield)
resources.reach: 1230: farmers already boil the spring water in pots for salt
resources.d: Known salt-making place of the period. Salt licks for cattle and salt to trade.

resources.qty: modern: small salt pan (guess on size)
resources.reach: 1230: salt crust scraped up in the dry season
resources.d: The 'salt pan mountains'. The nearest salt to Mapungubwe for cattle licks in the first years.

resources.qty: modern: ~70% of the world's chrome ore; layers of chromite up to ~1–2 m thick running for tens of km
resources.reach: 1230: black chromite bands crop out (as at Dwars River); easy to see, completely useless without electric furnaces or stainless steel
resources.d: A world treasure that is just black rock in 1230. Worth noting for the 1300s and beyond, not before.

resources.qty: modern: the Merensky and UG2 reefs hold roughly 75–90% of the world's platinum metals
resources.reach: 1230: the reef is a thin layer in hard rock holding only a few grams per tonne; invisible and unusable
resources.d: The richest platinum on Earth, and worthless here for centuries. Only matters once there's chemistry for catalysts.

resources.qty: modern: ~40% of all gold ever mined; reefs go down 4 km
resources.reach: 1230: thin outcrop of gold-bearing pebble rock at the surface; needs crushing and washing, low grade
resources.d: Gold close to the core, for buying horses and craftsmen at Sofala. He values it less than iron, but the coast only takes gold.

resources.qty: modern: quarried as 'black granite' and quartzite; effectively unlimited
resources.reach: 1230: boulders and outcrops everywhere along the Magaliesberg
resources.d: Hard stone for dams, mill stones and walls. Local people build in stone only without mortar; lime mortar changes that.

resources.qty: modern: open acacia and marula woodland across tens of thousands of km²; no big timber trees
resources.reach: 1230: firewood, poles and charcoal within a day's walk north of the core; the highveld to the south is treeless
resources.d: Enough for huts, carts and charcoal for a while, not for ships or a big iron industry. Why coal comes early.

resources.qty: modern: gone; historically huge herds of springbok, black wildebeest, blesbok, quagga and eland
resources.reach: 1230: herds in the tens of thousands on the open grass; hunted by San with bows
resources.d: Meat and hides for the first settlers. Eland can be tamed and milked, a possible extra draft animal.

resources.qty: modern: irrigated farms; the kingdom's cattle in 1230 are thousands of head (guess)
resources.reach: 1230: sorghum, millet and cowpeas on the river silt; hardy Sanga-type cattle that become plough oxen
resources.d: The food base at the start. Cattle are there from day one, so ox-ploughs and ox-carts need only iron and a wheel.

resources.qty: modern: small deposits, dug from caves in the 1800s–1900s (guess on size)
resources.reach: 1230: piles on cave floors in the dolomite hills (Cradle of Humankind area)
resources.d: Rich fertilizer and a source of saltpeter for later chemistry, right next to the core.

nearby.qty: modern: a small village; in the 1200s the southern end of the monsoon dhow trade
nearby.reach: 1230: ~3–4 weeks on foot from Mapungubwe; gold and ivory go out, cloth and beads come in
nearby.d: The one gate to the outside world. Horses, donkeys, wheat, paper and craftsmen can be bought here.

nearby.qty: modern: an archaeological site; a small trading beach town from the 700s
nearby.reach: 1230: occasional dhows; a smaller, older trading post south of Sofala
nearby.d: A second, quieter coastal contact point, nearer the southern route.

nearby.qty: modern: one of Africa's best natural harbours; rich fish and prawn grounds
nearby.reach: 1230: sheltered bay, fishing villages; dhows rarely come this far south
nearby.d: The closest good harbour to the core, down the escarpment. Site for his own port and shipyard.

nearby.qty: modern: ruins; in the 1200s the richest Swahili city, controlling the Sofala gold trade
nearby.reach: 1230: ~3–4 weeks by dhow from Sofala with the monsoon
nearby.d: Where the gold ends up and where cotton cloth, Indian goods, Arabic books and skilled craftsmen can be found.

nearby.qty: modern: ~30 million people; in the 1200s small trading towns and rice farmers (numbers unknown)
nearby.reach: 1230: by dhow across the Mozambique Channel; rice, zebu cattle, rock crystal, hardwoods
nearby.d: A source of rice, Asian crops and outrigger boat know-how. Its people's ancestors came from Borneo.

nearby.qty: modern: major fishing grounds and shipping lane
nearby.reach: 1230: monsoon winds take dhows north in Apr–Sep and south in Nov–Mar; currents and storms stop them south of Sofala
nearby.d: Sets the trading calendar. Ships come and go once a year with the wind.

nearby.qty: modern: Gujarat textile and port region; in the 1200s Cambay is a top port for cotton, beads and horses
nearby.reach: 1230: goods reach Sofala through Kilwa and Aden; a direct voyage takes a full monsoon season
nearby.d: Where horses, cotton cloth, beads, rice and shipwrights ultimately come from.

nearby.qty: modern: winter-rain farmland for wheat and grapes; a great harbour
nearby.reach: 1230: Khoekhoe herding land; no ship has ever come; ~1,300 km overland
nearby.d: The one part of the region with winter rain, perfect for wheat and vines. A later settlement and the sea road to the Atlantic.

nearby.qty: modern: ~57,000–60,000 ha, South Africa's largest forest; giant Outeniqua yellowwood, stinkwood, ironwood
nearby.reach: 1230: untouched; ~1,000 km away with no road, and the lagoon mouth is dangerous for ships
nearby.d: The only big ship timber in southern Africa. A later shipyard site once roads or coastal shipping exist.

nearby.qty: modern: Sishen is one of the world's big high-grade hematite mines (~1 billion t; guess)
nearby.reach: 1230: rich red and shiny hematite at the surface; local people already mine specularite for cosmetics (since ~800 AD)
nearby.d: Even richer iron than Thabazimbi, but far out on dry land with no fuel. A later resource.

nearby.qty: modern: one of the world's largest salt flats (~16,000 km²); a soda ash and salt plant runs at Sua Pan
nearby.reach: 1230: salt and soda crust over huge areas in the dry season; far, dry country
nearby.d: Effectively unlimited salt and soda, if Tswaing ever runs short.

nearby.qty: modern: hundreds of old workings; Zimbabwe's main gold belt
nearby.reach: 1230: being dug in narrow pits and washed from rivers by plateau farmers
nearby.d: Where much of the coast's gold comes from. Great Zimbabwe's wealth rests on it.

nearby.qty: modern: a 550 km ridge holding the world's second-largest chrome and platinum reserves
nearby.reach: 1230: visible chromite seams, useless without modern industry
nearby.d: Same story as the Bushveld: huge value later, none now.

nearby.qty: modern: one of the world's largest untapped coking coal fields (billions of t)
nearby.reach: 1230: seams outcrop along the river; the Zambezi is navigable from here to the sea in the wet season
nearby.d: Coking coal on a navigable river to the Indian Ocean. A future second industrial base.

nearby.qty: modern: a mid-sized field of good coking coal (billions of t; guess)
nearby.reach: 1230: outcrops in river valleys among Nguni-ancestor farmers
nearby.d: Good coking coal closer to the sea than Witbank, but over the escarpment.

nearby.qty: modern: ~20,000 in Kruger Park; in 1230 likely many more (guess)
nearby.reach: 1230: hunted for ivory by lowveld people and traded to the coast
nearby.d: Ivory is the second export after gold. Over-hunting it would empty the lowveld.

newcomers.d: Same language family, same cattle and rainmaking culture. In this society people already move to strong, prosperous chiefs. They are the first and easiest joiners.
Cattle people losing their grazing to drought. Wells and hay make an offer they understand.

newcomers.when: as soon as the highveld cattle posts start, ~1245+
newcomers.d: They live around the future core and already make salt and iron. Small chiefdoms with no big king join easily.

newcomers.when: Moloko pottery appears ~1300–1350; where they came from is unknown
newcomers.d: The people who historically fill the highveld from the 1300s and later build stone towns there. Cattle people with chiefs and age-sets, close enough in culture to join a water-rich kingdom.

newcomers.when: uncertain; Nguni-like groups reach the highveld maybe in the 1400s
newcomers.d: Cattle farmers from the wetter coast. Related culture, but a different language branch and strong local chiefs.

newcomers.when: from the 1250s, as iron and copper works grow
newcomers.d: Hired or invited to the core with land and cattle. Their skills are worth more than their numbers.

newcomers.n: San and Khoe hunters and herders
newcomers.d: Very different ways of life and languages. Many would trade or serve as trackers and herders rather than settle. Fair dealing matters.
Shipwrights, weavers, glassmakers and masons for pay and land. Muslim, literate in Arabic, used to cities. Kept in a few workshops.
People enslaved in the Indian Ocean trade, bought at the coast and given land and freedom inland. Mostly Bantu-speaking Africans, so the culture is close.

neighbors.d: Same culture as Mapungubwe, just starting its stone walls. By 1250 it is a growing gold-trade center and later takes over the coast trade when Mapungubwe falls. A rival for people and trade, not an army.

img.cap: Walls of Great Zimbabwe's Hill Complex on granite cliffs

neighbors.d: Cattle chiefdoms in eastern Botswana, past their best and fading by ~1300. A source of joiners, not a threat.

neighbors.pop: a few hundred to ~2,000 traders and locals (guess)
neighbors.d: A Swahili trading town under Kilwa's influence (the date Kilwa took control is disputed, ~1190s–1300). Dhows can't sail much further south. Traders seldom go inland, which helps keep secrets.

neighbors.pop: ~10,000–20,000 in the city at its peak (guess)
neighbors.d: The richest Swahili city, Muslim, ruled by the Shirazi dynasty and then the Mahdali from the late 1200s. It wants gold and ivory and has no interest in conquering the interior. Ibn Battuta visits in 1331.

img.cap: Ruins of the Great Mosque at Kilwa Kisiwani

neighbors.d: Trading towns of the coast linked to Arabia, Persia and India. Rivals of Kilwa, and other buyers if Kilwa's terms get bad.

neighbors.pop: unknown; small towns like Mahilaka plus rice farmers inland (guess)
neighbors.d: Malagasy-speaking people of Austronesian origin with Muslim traders on the northwest coast. Mahilaka is declining in this period. Harmless, and useful for rice and boats.

neighbors.pop: tens of thousands across the south and west (all Khoekhoe ~50,000–200,000 by the 1600s, disputed)
neighbors.d: Herders of cattle and fat-tailed sheep with no towns or iron-smelting. No outsider reaches them until the Portuguese in 1488. Peaceful trade is possible; land disputes are the risk.
Arab, Persian and Gujarati merchants who carry horses, cloth and beads. Their only interest is gold and ivory. None of them come inland, and Europeans don't appear until ~1500.
